explanations.explanation: The earth it is, friend. Ezekiel says, "…the earth shone with His glory." Think about that. Not a spotlight on one building, the whole earth lit up.

Close, friend, since the temple is where this is headed. But the text says "…the earth shone with His glory." not the walls. At this point the glory is still coming from the east. A few verses later, Ezekiel says the glory of the LORD filled the temple (Ezekiel 43:5).

I love a good night sky, believe me. My whole bakery sits under one. But Ezekiel doesn't mention the sky at all here. He says "…the earth shone with His glory." So the glow is down here, on the ground.

That's it, friend. Ezekiel says, "I fell facedown…" He's seen this kind of vision before, by the River Kebar and when He came to destroy the city, and he still goes straight to the ground. Facedown is how he meets the glory.
Not quite, friend. The text doesn't say Ezekiel turns away. He says, "I fell facedown…" That's what he does in front of the glory.

I can see why you'd pick it, because a sight like that could make anybody holler. I think I would. But the text doesn't give Ezekiel any cry here. It says, "I fell facedown…" No words from him at all, just down on the ground.

True, friend. Ezekiel says, "…the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east." He's facedown on the ground while it happens. The glory comes in by the very gate where the man brought him back to.

That one's actually true, friend. Ezekiel says, "…the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east." It comes from the east and goes in by the gate that faces east. The glory enters while Ezekiel is still facedown.

The Spirit it is, friend. Ezekiel says, "…the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court…" Facedown one moment, lifted and brought into the inner court the next. The Spirit is the one who does it.

explanations.answer: The man with the measuring rod
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd say it, since that man has been walking Ezekiel everywhere. But Ezekiel says it plainly: "…the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court…" The man is still around. In verse 6 he's standing beside Ezekiel. This particular lift just isn't his.

Angels are a fair guess, friend. I've met one myself, the angel who called me out of that drawer. But no angel is named here. Ezekiel says, "…the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court…" So the credit goes to the Spirit.
That's the one, friend. He says, "…where I will dwell among the Israelites forever." The throne, the soles of His feet, and then the promise to stay. That word "forever" is the big one.

explanations.answer: Rule from there for a season
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the voice doesn't mention a season. He says He will dwell among the Israelites "forever." There's no time limit in what He tells Ezekiel. This is a promise with no end date.
I get it. A throne makes you think of judging. But the voice doesn't say that here. He says, "…where I will dwell among the Israelites forever." What He promises about this place is staying.

Not quite, friend. The voice says the opposite. They placed their threshold next to His threshold, and "…they defiled My holy name by the abominations they committed." Then He says, "Therefore I have consumed them in My anger." Overlooking is not what happened.

False is right, friend. Nothing got overlooked. The voice says, "…they defiled My holy name by the abominations they committed. Therefore I have consumed them in My anger." It's a heavy part of the passage, and He says it plainly.

Ashamed is right, friend. He says, "…describe the temple to the people of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities." Then He adds, "Let them measure the plan…" In verse 11 He says, "…if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple…"

That's a good word, friend, and cleansing does show up later in this chapter, when the altar gets cleansed. But in verse 10 the word is "ashamed." He says the people may be ashamed of their iniquities. Cleansing isn't the goal named there.
Warned makes sense, friend, but it isn't the word in the text. Ezekiel is told to describe the temple "…so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities." The word is "ashamed."

True, friend. The voice says, "…if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple…" Then He adds, "Write it down in their sight…" The people get to see it in writing, so they can keep the whole design and carry it out.

That one's true, friend. The voice says, "…if they are ashamed of all they have done, then make known to them the design of the temple…" Then comes, "Write it down in their sight…" It's written where the people can see it, so they can keep its design and carry it out.

Most holy it is, friend. The voice says, "All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy." Then He says, "Yes, this is the law of the temple." The law covers all the temple's surrounding territory, not just the building.

explanations.answer: It will belong to the king
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, friend, but the law says nothing about a king owning it. It says, "All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy." Then the voice closes with, "Yes, this is the law of the temple."

explanations.answer: It will be open for trade
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. The law of the temple says, "All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy." Nothing in it opens that ground for trade. The voice ends with, "Yes, this is the law of the temple."

Accept is right, friend. The Lord GOD says, "Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD." It comes after the seven days of atonement for the altar, when the priests present the burnt offerings and peace offerings. It's a good place to end the chapter.
I can see why a test might come to mind, friend, but it isn't in this verse. After the seven days, the Lord GOD says, "Then I will accept you…" Acceptance is what He says comes next.

I'm glad that isn't it, friend. The earlier verses were heavy, so it's a fair worry. But the Lord GOD ends with, "Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD." Nothing in this verse scatters anybody.
